title: Direct Air Capture Integration at Sea: Learning from Terrestrial Geoengineering Failures
text:
Initial concepts of climate intervention heavily focused on land-based direct air capture (DAC) facilities, typically modeled as stationary industrial complexes. These precursor theories, while theoretically sound in capturing atmospheric CO₂ through chemical scrubbers, invariably ran into profound infrastructural limitations concerning energy supply and material logistics at planetary scales. The enormous electrical demand required to run DAC units—particularly for the energy-intensive processes of sorbent regeneration—proved to be a limiting factor when considering global deployment without destabilizing existing power grids.

The major failure point in these terrestrial models was resource confinement: the sheer land footprint, coupled with the inability of finite continental resources to sustainably supply both the necessary vast power inputs and the required chemical reagents. This structural bottleneck led researchers and policy makers to pivot from treating DAC as a purely terrestrial manufacturing process, towards coupling it with large, untapped environmental sinks. The deep ocean, providing immense heat dissipation capacity and geological storage potential, emerged as the natural solution set.

This recognition—that atmospheric mitigation required an integrated marine platform—was key. Integrating DAC at sea leverages the stability of maritime power sources (like offshore wind or tidal energy) and provides direct access to deep-water repositories for mineralization. Thus, DACIS represents not merely a location change, but a strategic operational pivot designed to bypass the insurmountable spatial and energetic constraints imposed by pure land-based climate engineering concepts.
